analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal regulator dedicated to banning unsafe consumer financial products like predatory loans.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a Financial Product Safety Commission — a standalone federal agency whose only job would be watching consumer financial products: loans, deposit accounts, payment services, and add-on products. It could write rules banning predatory or abusive practices, require clear disclosures, investigate industry practices, run a consumer complaint hotline, and fine or prosecute violators, with individual executives on the hook for knowing violations. The bill was Durbin's version of a 'product safety' approach to finance — the idea that a credit card or mortgage should be safe to use the way a toaster is.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers and small businesses that use credit cards, mortgages, bank accounts, and other everyday financial products. The bill would give them a dedicated regulator empowered to ban abusive fees and terms, a hotline to report problems, and the right to sue violators for damages and attorney fees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers and small businesses using credit

how_it_helps.text: Creates a five-member independent commission that can write binding rules banning 'abusive, fraudulent, unfair, deceptive, predatory' products and practices, and can restrict product features that push consumers into debt they cannot repay [S3].

Requires lenders to extend credit based on the borrower's ability to repay, protects consumer credit history and privacy, and lets the commission collect and publicize consumer complaints through a national hotline [S3].

Gives consumers a private right to sue for actual damages, twice the finance charge (minimum $1,000), plus attorney fees, and lets state attorneys general sue on residents' behalf — while leaving stronger state consumer laws and remedies fully intact [S3].
Bars anyone employed by or financially invested in a company selling consumer financial products from serving as a commissioner, so the watchdog cannot be staffed by the industry it watches [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks, credit card issuers, mortgage lenders, and other consumer financial product providers would bear new compliance costs, disclosure obligations, data demands, civil and criminal penalties (including up to $500,000 in criminal fines per knowing violation and personal liability for executives), and the loss of profitable but abusive fee structures.

drawbacks.text: The commission's jurisdiction covers essentially every form of credit, deposit, and payment, and it may even require a provider to sell it a financial product at cost so it can study the product firsthand — an unusually broad grant of power that even supporters of consumer regulation might find excessive [S3].

Its funding is 'such sums as may be necessary' with no dollar cap, so Congress would have little control over the agency's budget, and new compliance costs imposed on lenders could be passed along to borrowers as higher prices or reduced access to credit [S3].

Layering a new regulator on top of the Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC, credit union regulator, and FTC risks overlapping authority and conflicting rules, though the bill addresses this by superseding less protective rules and coordinating rulemaking [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but lopsided: consumers gain a watchdog with teeth — banning authority, hotline, lawsuits, executive liability — while lenders gain, as the bill's own title says, 'more regulatory certainty' in place of a patchwork of weaker, scattered rules. The costs are genuine compliance burdens and the risk of reduced credit availability at the margins, but the bill was deliberately designed (state-law floor, penalty-fund restitution, industry-free commission) to push costs onto abusive practices rather than ordinary lending.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee on March 10, 2009, and the committee never acted on it — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — for the rest of the 111th Congress.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on March 10, 2009, joined by Senators Schumer and Kennedy as original cosponsors [S3][S4].
Five other Senate Democrats and the chamber's lone Independent also cosponsored, for a total of six cosponsors — no Republicans signed on [S4].

The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day, and the bill's action history shows no further action of any kind for the remainder of the Congress [S1][S5].

The committee's inaction coincided with the Senate taking up financial regulatory overhaul as a broader bill in 2010, and the core idea of a dedicated consumer financial regulator was enacted that year in a different form, as the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau — so the death of this specific bill did not mean the idea went nowhere.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The consumer-regulator idea was largely carried into law through the 2010 financial overhaul rather than this bill, but the bill itself died without a vote — which was the outcome banks and consumer lenders preferred, sparing them a standalone commission with power to ban predatory products and personally penalize executives. In the short term, the lending industry was better off because the bill never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Lenders; consumers partly via later CFPB law

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats and the chamber's one Independent backed the bill — 6 of the 59 D/I senators cosponsored — and no Republican ever signed on; no votes were ever held, so party positions were never formally tested.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and mortgage lenders
industries.note: A standalone commission with power to ban predatory products, demand customer and revenue data, and impose per-violation civil and criminal penalties would directly attack revenue from overdraft fees, add-on products, and loose underwriting. Consumers' gain (fewer abusive products) is precisely the industry's loss.

industries.industry: Payday and other high-cost subprime lenders
industries.note: These lenders operate on product structures the commission would be empowered to ban outright as predatory, and the bill's private right of action would expose them to suits on every transaction.

industries.industry: Consumer financial products industry as a whole
industries.note: The bill's own stated purpose includes giving providers 'more regulatory certainty,' and it would help compliant providers develop safety standards and replace a scattered multi-agency patchwork with one set of rules; the cost is compliance, disclosure, and enforcement exposure.
